claim: Let \(\mathcal S\subset\mathbb C^3\) be the quartic surface from Gesmundo–Meroni, Example 3.2, defined by \(F=x_1^4-2x_1^2x_2^2+x_2^4+2x_1^2x_3^2+2x_2^2x_3^2+x_3^4-4x_3^2\). With \(u=x_1+x_2\), \(v=x_1-x_2\), and \(w=x_3\), one has \(F=(u^2+w^2)(v^2+w^2)-4w^2\). The reduced singular locus of \(\mathcal S\) is exactly \(V(u,w)\cup V(v,w)\), two transverse affine lines. On either line, away from the origin and the four points \((x_1,x_2,x_3)=(\pm1,\pm1,0)\), the completed local germ is an ordinary double curve \(\mathbb C[[s,X,Y]]/(XY)\). At each of those four points it is a pinch point, analytically equivalent to \(V^2-SW^2=0\). At the origin it is instead analytically equivalent to \(W^2-U^2V^2=0\): two smooth local branches tangent to the same plane, meeting along the two singular lines. Thus the named quartic boundary has exactly four pinch points, and the origin is a distinct tangential two-branch collision where its two double curves cross.
integrity: The proof is self-contained and the packaged exact verifier checks the coordinate identity, gradient, off-line saturation, transverse Hessian, pinch coordinate test, and origin discriminant.
scientific_limitations: Affine complex-analytic classification only; projective singularities at infinity and intersections with the four plane boundary components are not classified. A classically equivalent quartic under unrelated coordinates remains a residual literature risk.
title: Singularity stratification of the two-disc quartic boundary
